subject: Physics
central_question: How do stress, strain and elastic moduli quantify the way solids deform and recover under applied forces, and how are these ideas used in engineering design?
in_scope_units: 8.1 Introduction — elasticity, plasticity and engineering importance.
8.2 Stress and strain — longitudinal, shearing and hydraulic forms.
8.4 Stress–strain curve — proportional region, elastic limit, yield, plastic deformation, ultimate strength and fracture.
8.5 Elastic moduli — Young’s modulus, shear modulus, bulk modulus, Poisson’s ratio and elastic potential energy.
8.6 Applications of elastic behaviour of materials — ropes, beams, columns and limits on mountain height.

known_pitfalls.claim: A material that stretches more under the same load is more elastic.
known_pitfalls.correction: In the chapter’s elasticity convention, a larger Young’s modulus means greater elasticity or stiffness: less strain for the same stress.

known_pitfalls.claim: Stress is a vector because force is a vector.
known_pitfalls.correction: Stress is not assigned a single vector direction; it is characterised with reference to the surface and type of deformation.

known_pitfalls.claim: Hooke’s law is valid throughout the stress–strain curve.
known_pitfalls.correction: Hooke’s law applies only in the initial linear region where stress is proportional to strain.

known_pitfalls.claim: Bulk modulus is only for solids.
known_pitfalls.correction: Bulk modulus applies to solids, liquids and gases; Young’s and shear moduli require solid shape/length.
